Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
Fresh data points from September showed the housing market continues to deteriorate just as the Federal Reserve is considering raising interest rates again.
Building permits, new starts and pending sales all were considerably worse than Wall Street forecasts.
Under some circumstances, Fed officials would use easier policy to spur demand. However, the central bank is currently battling inflation, which it could prioritize over a flagging housing picture.
Workers install roofing for a new home under construction in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, June 29, 2026.
The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist.
Housing data deteriorated further in September , according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates.
Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage.
"The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze."
The National Association of Realtors reported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%.
Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday.
Pending home sales drop 7.3% in September, missing estimates
Privately owned housing starts fell 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data.
Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023.
"Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates."
The rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily . Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices.
Outside of the pending sales number, home builder sentiment is at lows not seen in 14 years.
Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs.
But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control. Readings last week on consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009.
Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing.
However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday.
"In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months."
Several data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. Goldman forecasts residential investment to decline 2.5%, 4% and 1%, respectively, over the coming three quarters, with a possibility for a steeper decline if mortgage rates don't fall.
The firm sees single-family starts of just 875,000 in 2027, little changed from this year, while existing sales are forecast at 3.9 million, also about the same as 2026 but notably 26% below pre-Covid 2019 levels. Walker attributed the middling levels as a product of the "lock-in" effect in which it's too expensive for current homeowners to move and take on higher borrowing costs while deteriorating affordability weighs on new construction.
"Housing activity has remained rangebound in recent years, capped on the upside by affordability headwinds and buffered on the downside by the longstanding housing shortage," Walker wrote. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity."
Markets expect the Fed to hold benchmark rates steady when it meets next week. However, futures pricing implies a strong chance of a quarter-point hike in December and another in March 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
One point of optimism comes from Yun, the NAR economist, who thinks the trend of mortgage costs running ahead of Fed hikes could mean that rates are topping out.
"Given that mortgage rates have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve's short-term interest rate hikes, mortgage rates could be topping out," he said. "Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably."

items.content:
Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there
By Stefanie Glinski ; photographs by Mohammad Mohsenifar in Bandar Abbas/on Hormuz Island
Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.
In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.
He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home
Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.
Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.
Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.
Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.
According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.
Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel .
With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.
But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.
Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street
Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.
Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption
Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.
“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.
Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas
“This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.
Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.
Hassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight years
Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.
A group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz Island
Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.
The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.
Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict
The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war
“The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.
The Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractions
From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.
Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.
Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.
“Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”

No wonder the White House wants Warsh to cut: A 1% Fed rate hike costs the Treasury an extra $95 billion a year in national debt interest
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (left) speaks with U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh during the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors’ meeting in Asheville, N.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Allison Joyce / AFP via Getty Images
There are many reasons—none particularly surprising—that politicians and policymakers push central banks for a lower base interest rate. It makes borrowing cheaper and stimulates the economy, potentially leading to more jobs and home purchases.
It also, conveniently, makes the government’s own borrowing costs cheaper.
While leaders the world over have lobbied for lower base rates for these reasons, none have done it quite so forcefully as President Donald Trump and his team. First, they went to extraordinary lengths—including personal insults and a criminal investigation—against previous Fed chairman Jerome Powell, and now the broader Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) led by new chairman Kevin Warsh.
Trump and his team have suggested that rates are too high, hurting consumers’ chances of owning a home as a result (mortgage rates are tied to long-dated rates). But Bank of America has also put a figure on the cost to the government of elevated interest rates.
“Clients are concerned about U.S. fiscal deficit risks. We are too,” wrote BofA analysts Meghan Swiber, Stephen Juneau, Mark Cabana, and Ralph Axel. “Higher rates become increasingly costly the longer they persist. The near-term deficit outlook has changed little, but the rates backdrop has changed the longer-run fiscal math.
“Higher yields compound into materially greater interest expense and Treasury financing needs over time, while raising the risk that the eﬀective interest rate on the debt eventually exceeds nominal growth. Debt spiral starts when interest costs exceed nominal growth.”
Treasury payments to service the $40 trillion national debt surpassed $2 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, the department recently announced.
In a recent analysis , the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) forecast the alterations to projected service payments on the debt under two interest rate scenarios. In the first, rates were 150 basis points higher than current projections between 2026 and 2036, and in the second, rates were just 50 basis points higher.
In the first scenario, in which interest rates are 1.5% higher than forecasts, deficits are $6 trillion larger, with a $4.9 trillion increase in net interest costs. A 0.5% increase results in $1.9 trillion added to current debt projections, with an extra $1.6 trillion added in net interest costs.
“Even if primary deficits remain largely unchanged, the growing interest burden materially increases the government’s financing needs,” the analysts wrote.
“We estimate that interest expense rises $95 billion a year for every 100bps of Fed hikes,” the team wrote.
Bank of America and its clients aren’t the only ones concerned that the U.S. fiscal picture is at something of a tipping point.
Over the weekend, Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s, wrote that global investors are digesting the U.S. spending habits and “appear to be demanding a higher rate to compensate for the mounting risk.”
He explained: “The 10-year Treasury yield is up about a percentage point this year, among the biggest increases of any major economy, and the countries with the heaviest interest burdens have generally seen the biggest increases.
“A vicious cycle threatens to take hold, with higher rates adding to the interest payments and debt load, which in turn pushes rates up even more.”
BofA’s team seems inclined to agree, writing that the bottom line means an unchanged deficit picture is becoming a “bigger financing problem.” They added: “As elevated yields feed through to the debt stock, interest expense compounds, financing needs rise, and the fiscal trajectory becomes less sustainable.”

items.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
items.summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
items.content:
By Rachel Clun Business reporter ,Â  Reporting from New York
US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.
The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.
The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.
The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.
Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.
"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.
The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.
That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".
The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.
It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.
Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.
"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.
The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.
"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.
The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.
It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.
Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

Breaking Nvidia unveils plans to build data center the size of shipping container
Gold Declines Towards $4,120 as Iran Conflict and Federal Reserve Outlook Remain in Focus
Gold coin ©PIX1861 Gold prices declined on Wednesday as investors assessed uncertainty surrounding efforts to end the conflict between the United States and Iran, alongside expectations for US interest rates and the potential inflationary effects of higher energy costs.
At 02:36 ET (06:36 GMT), spot gold was down 0.2% at $4,117.31 per ounce, while US gold futures fell 0.2% to $4,134.92 per ounce.
Other precious metals also traded lower. Silver declined 1.2% to $57.2955 per ounce, platinum lost 1.8% to $1,627.45, and spot palladium decreased 1.6% to $1,088.40.
The US Dollar Index edged up 0.1% to 101.80, adding to the market conditions affecting dollar-denominated commodities.
Gold has fallen more than 1% since the beginning of the week and remains approximately 20% below its level when the US-Iran conflict began in late February.
The conflict has disrupted energy supplies and contributed to higher oil prices, complicating the inflation outlook and expectations for monetary policy.
Higher interest rates can affect demand for gold because the metal does not generate interest income, making interest-bearing assets comparatively more attractive.
Oil Price Movements Reflect Uncertainty Over Iran Negotiations
Oil prices stabilised on Wednesday after retreating from a five-month high during the previous session.
The decline followed reports suggesting that diplomatic efforts could lead to an agreement to end the conflict. However, a diplomat subsequently dismissed suggestions that a settlement was imminent.
Gold prices initially increased as oil declined following the reports of possible negotiations, before reversing those gains when energy prices recovered.
The US dollar and government bond yields also moved lower during the period of fluctuating oil prices.
Market participants continued to assess the potential implications of the conflict for global energy supplies, inflation and economic activity.
The relationship between energy prices and inflation expectations remains particularly relevant to gold, given the influence of monetary policy expectations on demand for non-interest-bearing assets.
US Treasury securities with longer maturities gained as oil prices retreated and economic data indicated softer conditions in parts of the US economy.
September housing starts declined, while pending home sales fell to a record low, providing further evidence of reduced activity in the housing market.
The figures added to the economic information being considered ahead of the Federal Reserve's next monetary policy meeting, scheduled for 27–28 October.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's comments on Friday did not materially change market expectations for the upcoming decision.
Investors continued to anticipate that the central bank would leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged at the October meeting.
Market pricing indicated a probability of less than 17% that the Fed would increase rates by 25 basis points at that meeting.
However, inflation remains above the central bank's 2% target, and traders were assigning approximately an 85% probability to another interest rate increase before the end of the year.
Warsh's remarks came ahead of the Federal Reserve's communications blackout period, which begins on Saturday and restricts public commentary from policymakers before the meeting.
With limited additional guidance expected from central bank officials, investors are monitoring economic indicators, Treasury yields and developments in the Middle East for information that could influence interest rate expectations.
Gold and other precious metals remained under pressure during Wednesday's trading as markets continued to evaluate the interaction between energy prices, inflation and the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

‘A powerful warning’: will Europe’s angry protests lead to real political change?
Hamstrung governments seem to have no answer to the public’s furious demands, making further discontent likely
I n France , it was the piles of wheelie bins stacked up against school entrances that first hinted at the scale of student anger over crumbling classrooms and teacher shortages. In Spain, it was a tent camp that steadily grew in the heart of the capital as residents railed against soaring housing costs.
Similar scenes have since sprung up in Belgium, Italy and Portugal , and clashes have convulsed Albania’s capital of Tirana, hinting at an autumn of protests across Europe.
Much of the news coverage in recent days has focused on the violence that played out on the fringes of the protests in France and Italy . The protests themselves, however, point to what seems to be a diverse response to a common crisis: the growing perception, particularly among younger generations, that governments are unable, or unwilling, to deliver when it comes to affordable housing, social equality and robust public services.
graphic “This is the most powerful warning from Europe’s angry youth today, in France and across the continent,” the policy analyst Alberto Alemanno said.
The framing stands in sharp contrast to the many rightwing and far-right voices who have sought to exploit the violence in France and Italy, linking it without evidence to migration while brushing over protesters’ wider demands.
Officials in France have dismissed any link between the violence and immigration. The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, said on Sunday that the “unbridled violence” had been carried out by French people.
France protests escalate with riots, looting and 2,400 arrests - The Latest
Alemanno, a professor of EU law at the HEC business school in Paris, said he had received an unprecedented number of calls from right-wing, xenophobic outlets in recent days, many of them seeking to fuel the idea of the protests as some sort of “pan-European revolt”.
It is a narrative that he describes as misleading. “The demonstrations have different causes and do not necessarily share political objectives,” he wrote this week . “Yet their rapid spread hints at a common weak point: too many young Europeans doubt that existing institutions can deliver the security, opportunity and voice they expect.”
The head of the Paris office of the European Council on Foreign Relations, Célia Belin, said some of those doubts were currently being reinforced in France.
“Faced with the high discontent of young people in high school, the government has no answer for them,” she said, citing an administration squeezed financially by a high deficit and debt-to-GDP ratio and limited politically by the country’s deadlocked parliament. “Basically the answer is: ‘There’s no money, there is nothing we can do.’ And that’s a huge problem.”
graphic The view echoes that of the secretary general of France’s CGT union, Sophie Binet, after Saturday’s protests in which about half a million people turned up to rail against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services.
Binet condemned the violence, but she noted that the government had little choice when it came to quelling the protests. “Today’s mobilisation confirms the depth of the anger,” she said. “To get out of the crisis, there is only one way. Respond to the demands.”
Albania has also been shaken by mass student demonstrations for the past week after protests initially prompted by a proposal to build a resort backed by Donald Trump’s family.
In Milan, people took to the streets to protest against the rising cost of living, giving voice to the deep inequalities that now course through a city where an estimated one in 12 people is reportedly a millionaire .
graphic In Lisbon’s Rossio Square, housing campaigners set up camp on Saturday surrounded by banners that read “homeless generation” and “I just want a home to live in” and vowing to stay on as long as possible. It was an echo of the protests that have sprung up in Porto in recent weeks as residents push back against housing prices that more than doubled between 2015 and 2024, rising roughly twice as fast as the EU average.
The managing director for Europe at the consulting firm Eurasia Group, Mujtaba Rahman, said what had burst into public view was not a single, coordinated European movement. Instead the events of recent days had laid bare a “convergence of distinct national protest movements”, each with substantially different triggers.
Protesters camp out in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Photograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty Images “What links them is a growing perception that European governments are unable to deliver affordable housing, functioning public services and economic security, particularly for younger generations,” he said, citing a growing gap between public expectations and governments’ fiscal capacity.
“This mismatch between political demands and economic reality is likely to remain and grow over time, which suggests further discontent and protests are likely over the medium term,” he said.
Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs and a former Spanish foreign minister, went a step further when asked this month about the similarities between the housing protests in Spain and the school protests in France.
“The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” she told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “Young French people are protesting for education, young Spanish people for housing, but in Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
In Portugal, the campers were dislodged on Tuesday, leading to a fresh call for more housing protests. Similar calls for protests in the coming days have been heard across France, Spain and Italy, hinting at the tremendous task that lies ahead for officials across Europe, said Alemanno.
“They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold those responsible for criminal acts accountable, and address the underlying pressures, from housing costs and insecure work to strained public services and an uncertain technological future,” he said.
“Europe’s democratic institutions will be judged not by how forcefully they condemn disorder, but by whether they can turn generational anger into tangible political change.”

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Smartest Move Investors Can Make - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Smartest Move Investors Can Make  The Motley Fool
items.content:
After a year of record-breaking gains, major market indexes are wobbling. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.28% ) has fallen by nearly 2% over the last week, as of this writing, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.02% ) is down by more than 4% in that time.
Much of the sell-off is stemming from the tech sector, with artificial intelligence (AI) spending under the microscope. Rising bond yields have driven up borrowing costs, making it more expensive for AI hyperscalers to continue building data centers and related infrastructure. If big tech companies pull back on AI spending, it could cause a ripple effect across the broader market.
At this point, it's too soon to tell whether this volatility is a blip on the radar or the beginning of a deeper drawdown. Regardless of what's coming, though, Warren Buffett has one tried-and-tested strategy that can set your portfolio up for success.
In a 1999 essay for Fortune , Warren Buffett issued a warning to investors. The stock market was reaping the rewards of the dot-com boom, with the S&P 500 surging by nearly 200% over the previous four years, but Buffett predicted stock prices would fall.
He also emphasized that when an industry is poised to transform society, it's especially important to choose your investments carefully. Buffett mentioned airlines as an example, noting that while air travel itself has had a monumental impact on our lives, 129 airlines had filed for bankruptcy over the previous 20 years.
Buffett's 1999 warning eventually rang true, as the dot-com bubble officially popped in early 2000 -- leading to a bear market that would last more than two years. Hundreds of tech stocks crashed and burned, despite the internet's revolutionary impact on the world.
"The key to investing is not assessing how much an industry is going to affect society, or how much it will grow," Buffett said in the Fortune essay, "but rather determining the competitive advantage of any given company and, above all, the durability of that advantage."
When the dot-com bubble burst, overvalued stocks crashed the hardest. These companies earned explosive returns when the bubble was building, but many had unsustainable business models, poorly managed finances, or inexperienced leadership teams that couldn't navigate the bear market.
Now, we could be facing a similar situation. AI, as a technology, could transform the world. But not every company in the AI space will thrive. Many tech stocks have seen eye-popping returns this year, but it's likely that at least a few of them have been driven by hype and are overvalued right now.
This doesn't mean that all stocks will struggle over time, though. Since the start of the dot-com bear market in March 2000, for example, the S&P 500 has soared by more than 715%. While many companies failed, some tech stocks of the era -- like Apple , Amazon , and Microsoft -- went on to become industry-leading giants.
Overvalued stocks from weak companies will be hit the hardest whenever the next bear market arrives. Companies with strong fundamentals and a durable competitive advantage, however, have the best chance at recovering and going on to earn positive long-term returns.
The single best move investors can make right now is to load up on quality stocks. The healthier your portfolio, the more likely it is to survive even a severe downturn. In Buffett's words: "The products or services that have wide, sustainable moats around them are the ones that deliver rewards to investors."

Oil price today: WTI, Brent rise on Middle East worries
Oil prices climbed on Wednesday as escalating supply risks in the Middle East keep investors on edge.
Attacks on tanker near the Hormuz Strait and on Saudi Arabian facilities by Iran-backed Houthis have
Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 09, 2026.
Oil prices climbed Wednesday as worries over Middle East supply disruptions keep the market on edge, with attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy facilities denting sentiment.
Brent crude futures gained 0.86% to $109.73 a barrel as of 3:33 a.m. ET, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 0.78% to $98.58 a barrel.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that naval mines had prevented three tankers attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz using routes Tehran deemed unauthorized.
"Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," IRGC said in a statement published on their official Sepah News website .
Adding to regional worries, Yemen's Houthi militants claimed responsibility on Monday for strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Riyadh and Abha.
The escalating tensions have also sent global oil shipping costs soaring, adding another layer of pressure to energy markets.
The global average crude freight rate has surged above $20 per barrel, compared with just $3 a year earlier, according to a Goldman Sachs report published Tuesday. While rates have eased slightly in recent days, they remain roughly seven times higher than a year ago.
Goldman estimated that war-risk premiums associated with crossing the Strait of Hormuz accounted for about $7 of the $20 year-on-year increase in average crude freight rates, while ship-to-ship transfers outside the Persian Gulf contributed another $4.
The investment bank warned that elevated shipping costs could widen price differences between crude grades, squeeze refiners' profit margins and ultimately push up refined fuel prices.
"High freight costs have weighed particularly heavily on Asian refineries' net margins, threatening their refined product output, which could then raise global refined product prices," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote.

items.content:
Breaking Nvidia unveils plans to build data center the size of shipping container
US Stock Futures Edge Higher as SpaceX and Tesla Explore Merger and Meta Earnings Approach: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Wall Street NYSE stock exchange ©Shutterstock US stock futures traded mostly higher on Wednesday as investors assessed corporate earnings, developments in artificial intelligence investment and geopolitical uncertainty surrounding the conflict in the Middle East. Attention also turned to comments from Elon Musk about a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla, reports concerning Anthropic's financial performance and Meta Platforms' forthcoming quarterly results.
US futures rise as investors assess earnings and oil prices
At 03:01 ET (07:01 GMT), S&P 500 futures were up 13 points, or 0.2%, while Nasdaq 100 futures gained 148 points, or 0.5%. Dow Jones futures were broadly unchanged.
Wall Street ended Tuesday's session with mixed results. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced, while the Nasdaq Composite closed slightly lower.
Oil prices fluctuated during the session following unconfirmed reports that Qatar and Pakistan had proposed renewed negotiations aimed at ending the conflict involving Iran. Brent crude briefly declined from approximately $112 to $106 per barrel before recovering.
The initial decline in energy prices coincided with gains in equities, which have recently been affected by concerns over borrowing costs and the scale of debt-financed investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
"The relief from energy that played out late in the European session meant equities rallied as investors overcame some of their earlier AI jitters," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a research note.
Brent subsequently returned to approximately $110 per barrel after reports of comments attributed to Iran's president concerning the possibility of further US military action.
Technology shares underperformed parts of the broader market. An index tracking semiconductor companies declined 0.29%, although it recovered much of its earlier losses. AI cloud infrastructure provider CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) also rebounded during the session.
SpaceX and Tesla establish committees to examine possible merger
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) have formed committees to evaluate a potential combination of the two businesses, according to Elon Musk, who serves as chief executive of both companies.
Speaking to investors following SpaceX's quarterly earnings announcement, Musk said the committees had not reached an agreement on "the terms of any transaction."
Musk, who is not a member of either committee, said there was "no guarantee" that a merger would take place, although he considered there to be "a lot of merit" in combining the businesses.
Shares in both companies advanced in after-hours trading following the comments.
A potential transaction would bring together SpaceX's rocket launch and satellite operations with Tesla's electric vehicle and related technology businesses. No transaction terms or timetable have been announced.
SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, an increase of more than 160% compared with the previous year and above analysts' expectations.
The company recorded profit of $4.4 billion, while capital expenditure reached $19.6 billion during the period.
The results marked SpaceX's second quarterly earnings publication since its initial public offering earlier in 2026.
Tesla is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results after Wednesday's market close.
Anthropic reports revenue growth alongside financial and operational risks
Artificial intelligence developer Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANTP) reported substantial revenue growth during the first half of the year, according to media reports citing disclosures associated with its potential initial public offering.
The company, which develops the Claude AI models, generated revenue of $16.3 billion during the six-month period.
Approximately 20% of that revenue came from two customers, highlighting the concentration of sales among a relatively small number of clients.
Anthropic indicated that a significant proportion of its revenue is expected to remain dependent on a limited customer base for the foreseeable future.
The company also identified uncertainty surrounding access to the computing infrastructure required to develop and operate its AI models.
Anthropic recorded a net loss exceeding $80 billion, compared with a loss of $13 billion in the corresponding period last year. The reported increase was largely attributed to an accounting adjustment.
Additional risks identified in the disclosures included potential legal liabilities arising from the use of artificial intelligence, including cybersecurity-related incidents.
Reports suggested that a future stock market listing could value Anthropic at approximately $2 trillion, although no confirmed IPO valuation was provided.
Meta earnings to provide update on AI investment plans
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is scheduled to release its quarterly earnings after Wednesday's closing bell, with investors focusing on revenue performance and the company's spending plans for artificial intelligence.
The owner of Facebook and Instagram has recently expanded its AI product portfolio following the September introduction of its Muse model.
According to the reported information, the product attracted millions of downloads following its launch, with applications including travel booking assistance and tools for small businesses.
Meta subsequently introduced an open-weight version of its Muse Spark model for coding applications.
The earnings announcement will provide an update on Meta's investment requirements as it expands its AI infrastructure and related services.
Large technology companies have committed substantial capital to advanced semiconductor purchases, computing capacity and data centre construction as they develop AI products.
Investors have increasingly focused on the relationship between these expenditures, financing requirements and the revenue generated by AI-related services.
Meta's results will therefore be examined for information on capital expenditure expectations and the financial contribution of its AI initiatives.
Nvidia reportedly considers additional investment in Firmus Grid
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is in discussions about investing hundreds of millions of dollars in Australian AI cloud infrastructure company Firmus Grid, according to a report by The Information.
Nvidia already holds an investment stake in Firmus and has invested in several other companies operating in the AI cloud infrastructure sector.
The reported discussions follow Firmus Grid's decision to abandon plans for an initial public offering in Australia earlier this month.
The company cited recent financial market volatility as a reason for withdrawing the proposed listing, which it said would not have been in shareholders' interests under the prevailing conditions.
Firmus had previously outlined plans for an IPO at a valuation exceeding $30 billion, potentially making it one of Australia's largest stock market listings.
The size, structure and timing of any additional Nvidia investment have not been confirmed.
US equity markets entered Wednesday's session with attention divided between corporate earnings, AI infrastructure financing and developments in the Middle East. The forthcoming results from Meta and Tesla, together with reported activity involving SpaceX, Anthropic and Nvidia, are among the company-specific developments being assessed by investors.

A 2027 turning point? Goldman, Citi see stabilising signs in China’s housing market
Encouraging holiday sales and shrinking supply point to recovery for country’s property sector, according to Goldman Sachs and Citi
As China’s housing market downturn enters its fifth year, global investment banks including Goldman Sachs and Citi say they expect the sector to pivot as soon as 2027, with expectations fuelled by signs of shrinking supply and robust sales over the National Day holiday in early October.
Citi holds a positive view on the sector and saw 2027 as a pivotal year for home price recovery in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. Home prices in China hit their lowest point in June 2024, according to Citi.
Shanghai became the first city to post positive year-on-year growth in secondary home prices in September, with prices rising 0.8 per cent, according to the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday.
“While we need further confirmation before declaring a sustained recovery, the evidence increasingly points to stabilising and potentially rising home prices in top cities, with most tier-two cities likely to lag,” said Griffin Chan, an analyst at Citi Research, in a report on Tuesday.

Photograph: Valeria Ferraro/Anadolu/Getty Images A video of a lorry driver’s teenage daughter breaking down in tears has gone viral after she said her family could no longer afford to go out at weekends because they were struggling to pay their bills.
Italy’s infrastructure minister, Matteo Salvini, has proposed €430m in financial support, but the motorway blockades and lengthy traffic jams continue, putting the government under growing pressure as anger over the cost of living mounts.
The protests have also sparked criticism of Italy’s public broadcaster, Rai, which has been accused of giving greater prominence to violent student demonstrations in Milan than to the economic hardship facing families and lorry drivers in the south. Critics say the coverage plays into the government’s increasingly hardline approach to protests while diverting attention from the growing cost-of-living crisis.
Meanwhile, back to Witkoff’s meeting with Putin in St Petersburg, the US president, Donald Trump, has just welcomed the release of Stephen Hubbard, a US citizen held by Moscow on allegations of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine ( 11:24 ).
“Stephen Hubbard, taken four years ago by Russia during the Biden Administration, was just released from prison, at the request of President Donald J. Trump, made directly to President Vladimir Putin in a telephone conversation last week.
Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no “swap” necessary for this release.
This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin. Stephen is on his way back home. “Welcome home Stephen, it’s great to have you back,” stated President Trump.”
Familiar images of teargas clouds drifting across Paris squares, police baton charges against masked protesters and terrified teenagers floored – and worse – by stun grenades have once again focused the world’s attention on France’s policing methods.
Police forces present at a demonstration in Rennes, France. Photograph: Vernault Quentin/NurPhoto/Shutterstock While most of its western European neighbours generally favour police tactics that prioritise crowd containment and de-escalation, France has long responded to social movements that take to the streets with, at times, shocking physical force.
The reasons why are a complex mix of history, politics, state organisation and a particular security culture that has become deeply ingrained over decades, if not centuries, and whose limits continue to be pushed today.
French policing policy is rooted in Napoleon’s ultra-centralised state and in the political philosophy of the Republic. In France, the police are an instrument of the state. Their core task is to protect it, enforce its laws, and maintain public order.
Conceptually, that is a far cry from, for example, the UK, where since the early 1800s the police have been considered servants of the public, whose authority derives from public consent and whose chief responsibility is to keep the peace.
French police officers are agents of state authority. That means protests, blockades and mass disorder are not just civil nuisances, but direct challenges to the authority of the republic. The police’s priority is to reclaim the streets, not to negotiate.
That explains the aggressive tactics, such as systematically encircling and trapping crowds, and their continued use of “intermediate” or less-than-lethal weapons, many of which are banned or heavily restricted elsewhere in Europe.
Why are French police so violent? Their job is to protect the state, not the people
Meanwhile, French president Emmanuel Macron blasted “unacceptable” and “stupid” comments on the protests and riots in France from foreign leaders, accusing them of “campaigning at our expense.”
French President Emmanuel Macron speaks to members of the media in Qatar. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters Speaking to reporters from Doha, visibly annoyed Macron said he was frustrated by “visible manipulation of information” about the events in France, “that were unacceptable and stupid from many quarters, including from foreign leaders.”
“For instance, we saw images generated by artificial intelligence depicting scenes that never actually occurred in France. Some people even claimed that we had been overrun by hordes of migrants and Islamists – which is completely false.”
(US president Donald Trump explicitly suggested that, repeatedly, and several EU leaders sort of said similar things, linking the protests with migration, including Hungary’s Péter Magyar and Poland’s Donald Tusk. )
Trump attacks ‘migrants and communists’ as he tries to exploit France unrest
Macron said he was particularly annoyed by political leaders “whether in our own region or on the other side of the Atlantic, gullibly repeating claims generated by AI or echoing narratives that certain circles with to propagate … it is clear that they are campaigning at our expense.”
He said these comments “reveal who loves France and who does not.”
Macron said he would hold a meeting with ministers and intelligence officials on his return on Thursday to get a “detailed account” of what happened and preparations for this weekend’s protests.
We are getting some first lines from the Kremlin saying that Russia will analyse the US proposals, but “much depends on Ukraine .”
US envoy Steve Witkoff meet Russian president Vladimir Putin
“If Ukraine does not make necessary decisions, situation for them will be worse,” a quote attributed to the Kremlin and posted by the Interfax news agency said.
Russian president Vladimir Putin, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and other officials attend a meeting at the Constantine Palace in Saint Petersburg, Russia. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/Reuters The picture above is from Russian state-owned Sputnik news agency.
During their initial exchange, relayed via the Russian state news agency Tass, Putin reportedly said that he was interested in restoring ties and economic cooperation with the US, as he praised the diesel deal with Trump.
He also recalled Trump’s comments on the need to end the Russian war of aggression in Ukraine to stop the loss of human life, and asked about the talks in Oslo.
In turn, Witkoff said he hoped Putin would consider resuming peace talks with the US and Ukraine for “technical discussions,” and said the Oslo meeting was productive, with “a foundation in place to move toward a ceasefire.”
Let’s see if we get any more detail after the meeting.
It looks like the hosts had something special lined up for the US guests…
Russia has released an American man imprisoned on charges of fighting as mercenary in Ukraine , US envoy Witkoff says.
Agencies identify him as Stephen Hubbard, arrested in 2024.
Russian court sentences 72-year-old American for fighting for Ukraine
Witkoff is now talking to Putin, according to Russian state media.
The pair is meeting in Saint Petersburg’s Konstantinovsky Palace. Putin is joined by Dmitriev, who picked up Witkoff from the airport earlier.
We will no doubt hear and hopefully see more from the meeting shortly.
Overnight, a handful of Republicans have spoken out against Donald Trump ’s softening stance on Russia , threatening to pull financial support for his agenda over his “embarrassing” handling of the Ukraine war.
President Donald Trump is reflected in protective glass after speaking at a campaign rally at Pitt–Greenville Airport. Photograph: Matt Ramey/AP Don Bacon, an outgoing congressman in Nebraska, condemned Trump’s actions – which include a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel and the pausing of sanctions on Moscow – as “absolutely disgraceful” and accused the US president of cozying up to a “war criminal” in Vladimir Putin , his Russian counterpart.
“It really is disgraceful, and the Republicans that I associate with, there’s a lot of us, can’t stand it,” Bacon told CNN on Monday. “I think the president’s leverage in this Congress is shot.”
Last week, Trump waived sanctions imposed on Russia through a law named after his longtime ally and late senator Lindsey Graham. The legislation, which he signed only last month, was intended to increase financial pressure on Russia, more than four years after it invaded Ukraine.
Instead, Trump announced he had struck a deal with Putin to import diesel fuel, which has become more expensive for Americans largely due to Trump’s war with Iran. Trump has previously blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russia.
Republicans push back on Donald Trump’s wavering support for Ukraine
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ⁠anti-corruption police said ⁠that ⁠detectives were ​searching the premises of ⁠the National Bank of Ukraine ⁠and also ​the ‌home address of ‌one of ‌the central bank’s employees, Reuters reported.
The anti-corruption police said in a statement ‌on the Telegram app that ​no one has been detained or issued ⁠a suspicion notice. ​The central ​bank did ​not immediately ​respond ‌to ​a request ​for comment.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg early morning for talks with Russian president Vladimir Putin about Ukraine, a day after holding discussions with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders of Norway and Finland.
Witkoff was met at Pulkovo Airport by the Kremlin’s advisor for international economic cooperation, Kirill Dmitriev.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev greets US special envoy Steve Witkoff upon his arrival at Pulkovo Airport in Saint Petersburg, Russia. Photograph: Obtained by Reuters/Reuters Let’s see how much of the positive tone expressed by Zelenskyy and the two European leaders after yesterday’s talks will hold at the end of the day.
But managing out expectations, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said he “didn’t know if any agreement will be reached today,” Russian news agency Interfax said.
US has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says Zelenskyy
Elsewhere, I will be looking for updates from France and Italy, as both countries step up their response to recent protests and riots that disrupted everyday life.
Italy to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and looting
It’s Wednesday, 21 October 2026 , it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live .

items.title: Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
items.summary: The spire of the clock tower at Limoges city hall dramatically collapsed as it was engulfed in flames on Saturday.
items.content:
A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.
The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFM TV report.
French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has vowed a "massive" police presence during further protests planned for Saturday, while several cities, including parts of Paris, will be subject to curfews this week.
Marseille mayor BenoÃ®t Payan said on X that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew "starting this evening and for days to come", with French media reporting it would be in place overnight from Tuesday to Friday.
Payan said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.
Paris's police commissioner has also ordered the extension of an overnight curfew in the capital. The PrÃ©fecture de Police said the measure would continue "for as long as it proves necessary".
A curfew for parts of central Lyon was renewed on Tuesday, while overnight curfews for Nice and Lille are ongoing, and a week-long, overnight curfew for Bordeaux came into force on Tuesday night.
French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin told BFM Television that 149 people were in detention following widespread demonstrations over the weekend.
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Darmanin previously said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".
Lecornu told French parliament on Tuesday afternoon a large number of police would meet demonstrators at a planned protest on Saturday.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez previously admitted police had "lost control" in some cities over the weekend.
He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.
Image caption, The city hall's roof and clock tower in Limoges was severely damaged in the fire
Lecornu also accused far-left groups of an "insurrectionary" plan over the weekend's mass chaos.
Responding to an earlier, similar accusation from Lecornu, left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) de facto leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon had called for the prime minister to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder".
On Tuesday, MÃ©lenchon urged followers on social media to show "restraint" in the face of any "provocation".
Lecornu earlier said targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder.
Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.
Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced on Monday in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
A crowd assembled in Lyon on Monday night in support of businesses affected by the disorder but dispersed without violating the curfew, officials said.
The RhÃ´ne prefecture said on social media that it was "furious" that a far-right group tried to hijack the gathering. The prefecture said on X it reported the group to the public prosecutor for alleged Islamophobic and xenophobic remarks.
Image caption, The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday night
Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.
Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.
More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.
Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.
Image caption, Riots took place across French cities, including the capital Paris
More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.
Protest organisers earlier declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.
The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.
Meanwhile, French union La CGT has called for a major day of strikes on 5 November.

At 3pm BST / 4pm CEST Friday 23 Oct , Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from our readers about the riots and protests in France. Send your questions by email now to conversations@theguardian.com , or join the discussion on Friday

Alexander Hurst and Rokhaya Diallo. Composite: Guardian Design
The Hôtel de Ville in Limoges, central France, on fire during a weekend of unrest. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty Images After weeks of protests and a weekend of riots in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured, the repercussions for France – for its society and its economy – continue. Allegations of police brutality surfaced, and the violent protests unnerved investors, resulting in a debt sell-off , with borrowing costs rising higher than for Greece. All of this ahead of a hotly contested presidential election that’s now just six months away.
The French government’s escalating financial problems were covered by the Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley who wrote: “France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946 . Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.”
Columnist Paul Taylor commented that “Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel (Marine) Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy.”
And the Guardian’s editorial noted that “In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.”
What are your views on the riots, their causes and their aftermath? Are they paving a path to the presidency for Le Pen? In his final months in charge, can embattled incumbent Emmanuel Macron meaningfully address the situation in which France finds herself?
France-based Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live here at 1500BST on Friday 23 October to answer your questions on what happened, why, and where France goes from here.
Comments will open at 0900BST on Friday, but you can send your questions by email now to conversations@theguardian.com

US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in St. Petersburg. A US official told CNN Witkoff was visiting Russia to “test” whether a new peace plan can form the basis for peace talks.

US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff arrives in Russia ahead of talks with Putin
US special envoy Steve Witkoff held talks on Wednesday with Russian President Vladimir Putin aimed at advancing proposals to end to the war in Ukraine and create a pathway to broader negotiations .
The talks on Wednesday morning in St. Petersburg came off the back of Witkoff’s Tuesday summit with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway. In video of the beginning of the three-hour meeting with Putin, Witkoff said discussing the outcomes of that “productive” Oslo summit was on the agenda.
“I think there’s some degree of momentum, and I hope that this today can be another step forward in the peace process and discussing how we resolve the Ukrainian conflict,” the Trump administration envoy said.
Witkoff implored Putin to consider resuming trilateral Russia-US-Ukraine talks, where technical issues could be discussed, he said in the meeting. Putin expressed interest in the topic of restoring economic cooperation with the United States and the possibility of a meeting with China to discuss Ukraine.
A key outcome of the meeting was Witkoff announcing that Russia has released 74-year-old American prisoner Stephen Hubbard , who has been detained in the country for more than four years.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff meet inside the Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg on October 21.
Putin, Witkoff and translators sat around a large round table as they discussed a wide range of issues including Russia’s willingness to help resolve the war in Iran, potential Russian fertilizer exports to the US and the release of Hubbard. The meeting continued behind closed doors, and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law who has also been involved in the peace negotiations, joined remotely given he has the flu.
In this photo released by the Moscow City Court Press Service, Stephen Hubbard, a US citizen accused of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine against Russia stands in a glass cage during a court session in the Moscow City court on Monday, Oct. 7, 2024.
Russia frees 74-year-old American after visit from Trump envoy, state media reports
The US and Ukraine made “meaningful progress” in the Norway talks on Tuesday, a US official previously told CNN. Ukraine “brought forward new ideas and proposals, which were discussed in detail,” and the two sides are now in “strong alignment” on what the next steps will be, the official said.
“Discussions covered key elements of a comprehensive peace framework, including long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic and prosperity plan, and a broader European security architecture designed to create lasting stability,” the US official said.
Ukraine and its allies reiterated the key red lines set by Kyiv for any peace negotiations, including the need for future security guarantees – to ensure Russia doesn’t invade again – and a rejection of any demands to give up territory.
Russia has demanded that Ukraine gives up the entire eastern Ukrainian Donbas region, which is now mostly under Russian occupation. Moscow has also called for Ukraine to dramatically reduce the size of its military and pledge to never join NATO.
“We have some clear ideas on how to get to peace, and we are united with our European partners in this effort. And we want the Americans to take these ideas to the Russians,” Zelensky said on Tuesday. “Let’s see what Putin has to say.”
“Much depends on whether the American side will hear something new from Russia today – about peace, rather than the continuation of the war,” Zelensky added on Wednesday, following another meeting with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
Zelensky said that Ukraine also wants trilateral negotiations involving Trump, Putin and himself, but the process would be “better with Europeans.”
“I always said that we are open to negotiate in any format, any topics, but don’t speak about us without us, please,” he told Fox News on Wednesday, balking at the prospect of any Russia-China-US negotiations.
The Kremlin has previously shut down the idea of trilateral negotiations, apart from a previous invitation for Zelensky to come to Moscow – something viewed as unviable by the other sides.
Regarding the Norway talks with the Ukrainian side, the US official added: “The teams are working exceptionally well together, with a shared commitment to finding practical solutions to end the war,” striking a positive tone despite the souring public relationship between Zelensky and US President Donald Trump.
“The goal is to build on the progress made with Ukraine and Europe, discuss the proposals with Russia, and create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations,” the US official said.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev greets US special envoy Steve Witkoff upon his arrival at Pulkovo Airport in Saint Petersburg, Russia, October 21, 2026.
Meanwhile in Russia, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Tuesday struck a less upbeat tone, saying that Moscow will see what Witkoff brings to the table but will not make “political concessions.” Lavrov said that Moscow does “not expect a miracle” and Washington will remain a rival to Russia “at best,” according to Russian state media TASS.
A European official in Oslo told CNN: “I think plans – or lack of – isn’t as much of a problem as getting Russia to treat any plan seriously.”
CNN’s Anna Chernova, Ivana Kottasová, Kevin Liptak, Nick Paton Walsh and Kosta Gak contributed to this report.

items.summary: OpenAI will now have its models on all three of the top clouds, giving corporate developers more choice.
items.content:
OpenAI bring its AI models to Google's cloud, expands beyond Microsoft
OpenAI said its models will be available for developers through Google's cloud after years of competition between the two companies.
The ChatGPT maker will now have its models on the three major U.S. clouds.
Amazon started hosting OpenAI models in April after exclusivity ended with Microsoft.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman delivers a keynote speech during OpenAI's annual DevDay event in San Francisco, California, US, September 29, 2026.
OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.
For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers. That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.
Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property. The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models .
Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.
"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year. Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively. All three report quarterly results next week.
Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems. In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.
OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google. Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.
Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when the AI lab said it was using Google's cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface.
