items.content:
The key level traders are watching on the S&P 500 that could mean an even bigger decline is ahead.
Warren Buffett’s answer for how one should become inflation-resistant.
Investors' collective cash cushion against an adverse market surprise is running low.
Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE
In a previous life, when I routinely shut down New York City bars, the end of Daylight Saving Time was an annual bonus, as 2am on a Saturday night instantly became 1am, leaving three more hours until closing time.
The financial markets now are undergoing several forms of late-cycle unease, and Wall Street is now looking for earnings season and the passage of the midterm elections to turn back the clock before last call.
To be clear, this remains a bull market, the S&P 500 's uptrend unbroken, with constant rotations between AI tech and remainder of the market fitfully supporting the tape, with pullbacks limited to 3% for half a year.
Still, the index is now chopping around a flattish 50-day moving average at levels first reached 11 weeks ago, the AI-hardware cohort has badly broken stride, bank stocks are trading poorly off their results, and credit markets are getting colicky.
Late last week, the urgent selling in semiconductors and data-center equities and debt resembled the sort of forced-unwind rhythms from July, when a big upstart tech hedge fund was in the process of being all but liquidated.
A tentative bounce in semiconductor stocks Monday was minimally reassuring, in that it meant we didn't get the further disorderly purge many had braced for over the weekend (when S&P 500 "perpetual" futures on Hyperliquid had a sudden head-fake drop late Saturday).
Jason Hunter, technical strategist at JP Morgan, sets out the crucial question for a market sending mixed signals:
"With the bearish seasonal window now closing, we are left wondering if the market is in the terminal phase of a sequence of rolling corrections ahead of a typical late-year rally. Or are the plentiful amounts of bearish internal, momentum, and intra-market divergences that have formed as the S&P 500 index has decelerated below longer-term channel resistance setting the market up for a larger and more correlated setback?"
He leans toward a more cautious interpretation, keeping the S&P 500 on a short leash that extends about 2.5% lower to 7500, a break of which would lose the tape the benefit of the doubt.
Based on precedent and circumstance, the market "should" be setting up for a comeback that could reset the clock in bulls' favor. The fourth quarter after a midterm election year, historically, is overwhelmingly positive. Earnings growth projected to exceed a 20% year-over-year growth rate again this quarter can hardly be viewed as anything but a positive at least to bolster the fundamental case.
Still, against most probabilities, 2018 happened. By which I mean a 19% S&P 500 peak-to-trough decline in the fourth quarter of a midterm-election year, one that saw total S&P 500 earnings grow by more than 20%.
The 2018 tailspin had followed a massive momentum crescendo and reversal several months earlier, which gave way to an erratic tape that couldn't absorb what seemed at the time relatively unthreatening Federal Reserve tightening actions.
Financial conditions have now been tightening by means of higher Treasury yields, somewhat wider corporate-credit spreads, an uptick in volatility and a stronger U.S. dollar.
It's become common to hear investors insist that "the market is doing the Fed's tightening for it," suggesting Chairman Kevin Warsh himself should show restraint in further hiking rates despite the recent upturn in inflation. Sure, but the reason the markets are tightening is, in part, because Warsh himself expressed resolve in fighting inflation and investors therefore believe he'll take short-term rates up a bit more.
How Warsh treats these market shifts after next week's Fed meeting is another node of disagreement on the Street.
Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave says the markets are testing the Fed's pain threshold with the Nasdaq retreating 5% and credit spreads flaring a bit. The market has taken recent Fedspeak to suggest very low chances of an October rate hike, even though Warsh himself has decried forward guidance and said the Fed shouldn't suppress normal market volatility. Bhave is maintaining his non-consensus prediction for an October hike, conceding it's a close call.
Morgan Stanley equity strategist Mike Wilson takes the other side on the Fed's response to the recent tensing up of markets: "We think some acknowledgement of this tightening by Warsh would be well received by rate-sensitive areas that have already derated notably. Conversely, an indifference to this tightening may invoke memories of Powell's 2018 'auto-pilot' remarks in reference to that tightening episode."
The "de-rating" and "de-risking" process has surely been notable in recent weeks, with small and cyclical stocks under significant valuation pressure and hedge funds aggressively repositioning out of tech.
Is it enough to enliven buyers into or after the election?
Ned Davis Research thematic strategist Pat Tschosik notes his firm's proprietary market-breadth reading Big Mo Tape tentatively turning higher from oversold readings. "If Big Tech disappoints on Q3 earnings, we may get a full market washout and Big Mo could head even lower like it did in October 2023. Perhaps this is what is needed to set up for a post-midterm-election rally into yearend."
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors sees a similar level to JPMorgan's as the market's breaking point, while evaluating his sentiment indicator.
Kolovos on the latest reading: "A noticeable sentiment reset is underway on the heels of the AI trade unwind and tightening financial conditions.  The good news is that bullish sentiment is finally starting to wash out, which should set the stage for a year-end rally. However, a break below the mid-September lows on the S&P 500 near 7,500 would warn that something more than a routine pullback is unfolding."
-There's something of a paradox at work – or a collective investor blind spot - when the bond market is finally offering relatively safe income after many years of meager yields and yet people continue to rush for the engineered income delivered by options-selling ETFs. This CNBC.com piece offers a thorough, smart rundown of these strategies, complete with warnings of tax pitfalls. This Bloomberg report details a more aggressive approach through funds many investors don't quite understand, while introducing me to the community of self-styled "dividend nomads."
-Anthropic's proposal to place 5% of its equity into a "public benefit fund" to help groups potentially disadvantaged by AI's propagation and Elon Musk's stated offer to give one of his SpaceX shares to every American child via Trump Accounts suggest that anxiety over AI economic disruption is going from simmer to boil.
We can cynically observe that such efforts also hype these companies' world-changing potency, a form of marketing through scare-mongering sheathed in generosity.  But the concern over AI's impact on current worker groups is well-placed, even if ultimately society adapts around step-function technological change. The best hedge against AI-powered capital overtaking labor is arguably to own more capital, whether through the S&P 500 or other vehicles.
Or one could raise the value of one's human capital, through training or becoming excellent at something. This has always been Warren Buffett's answer for how one should become inflation-resistant,  as he detailed at Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting a few years ago , at the height of the pandemic inflation surge.
Bull markets can keep rolling for a long while after they've become fully embraced and stocks are no longer cheap. But I find myself cataloguing various ways that the cushions against adverse surprises are getting worn pretty flat.
Here's the running tally of investors' collective cash holdings as a percentage of total margin debt. It's running well below the levels of the year 2000 at this point.
Industry participants are quick to point out some extenuating factors: A massive jump in certain long-short tax-avoidance strategies that pushed up margin borrowing without representing true upside leverage. And investors these days often have their cash swept into bank deposits that might not be captured in this measure.
Still, whatever's driving it suggests high market exposures and a bit less cash buying power.
Here's a cut-to-the-chase relationship for comparing equities and bonds. Total shareholder yield – through dividends and share buybacks combined – now lags the yield on the 10-year Treasury note.
Not a bright flashing alarm, but a reason to assume that the hurdle rate for taking equity risk is a bit higher than it's been for most of the past 20 years.

Michigan AG criticizes Consumers Energy's new natural gas rate hike case days after MPSC approval
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel is criticizing Consumers Energy for announcing intent to seek a rate hike, just days after the Michigan Public Service Commission approved a rate hike.
According to the AG's office, the MPSC approved a $139 million natural gas rate hike for Consumers Energy on Thursday, Oct. 15, which was a 4.3% increase for a typical residential customer. The MPSC also approved a 9.8% return on equity, the utility's profit margin.
On Monday, the energy company submitted a filing announcement to seek another natural gas rate hike on or after Dec. 18, 2026.
Nessel said her office will file to intervene in the case.
“Consumers Energy was approved for a new natural gas rate hike just last week, and before a single new dollar could be spent, they’ve announced their next rate hike,” Nessel said in a statement. “Major utilities like Consumers Energy and DTE employ entire teams of staff to craft rate hike applications to file one right after another, and their bill paying customers pay all the costs to craft these massive proposals. In the past, we have asked the MPSC to require both companies to track their costs associated with rate hike cases and, as long as their customers are paying for the process, I hope someday soon we’ll know just how much.”
Consumers said on its website that the approved rate hike from Oct. 15 will take effect in November 2026, and businesses will see an estimated monthly increase of $25.29, and exact bills will depend on how much electricity you use.
"We deliver natural gas to over 1.8 million homes and businesses across Michigan. This responsibility requires ongoing work to build and maintain the infrastructure that brings energy right to you. We do this because we understand how important dependable energy is to your business," the Consumers website reads .
The company said that the funds will be used for replacing thousands of service lines, updating pressure facilities, adding cost-effective technology, replacing hundreds of miles of pipelines and more.
"Consumers Energy continues to work toward securing our natural gas system and ensuring safety, reliability and affordability for customers. The natural gas rate for Consumers Energy customers has fallen from $11.90/Mcf in 2022 to $11.03/Mcf in 2025 – or 7%, which means our natural gas rates have come down more than twice as much as rates across other Midwest energy providers. Consumers Energy remains focused on helping our friends and neighbors by offering money‑saving programs and connecting customers with assistance that can help manage bills. To help keep energy bills more predictable and manageable, Consumers Energy files smaller rate requests rather than waiting several years, when larger increases can be harder for customers," a statement from the company reads.

items.title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite new optimism
items.summary: The Ukrainian leader's hug with Steve Witkoff in the Norwegian capital is unlikely to dispel misgivings about US policy towards his country, writes Paul Adams.
items.content:
Image caption, Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capital
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close â that much is obvious â but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.
In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, using an expletive while criticising Benjamin Netanyahu's judgement. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."
Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"
For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.
But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."
Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.
"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.
After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.
The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.
One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.
Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.
Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports â not confirmed by US officials â come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.
Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.
Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.
Figure caption, Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.
Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.
"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.
Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".
For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.
Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation â again not confirmed by Washington â that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.
"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.
On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.
The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.
Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink .
A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.
Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.
It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink â or its military grade equivalent Starshield â originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.
Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."
But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.
Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.
Image caption, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabated
A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (Â£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.
Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain fromâ¦ digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.
Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

items.title: OpenAI Is Reportedly Raising $30 Billion. Which Chip Stock Gains the Most? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: OpenAI Is Reportedly Raising $30 Billion. Which Chip Stock Gains the Most?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
OpenAI is raising cash again. The ChatGPT maker is seeking around $30 billion in a round that might value it at over $1.4 trillion, Reuters said on Oct. 19. That's up from an $852 billion valuation in March. The talks are still ongoing, though, so nothing's closed.
For chip investors, the bigger number might be what OpenAI has already lined up. In 2025, it announced plans for 26 gigawatts of computing capacity with Nvidia ( NVDA -0.29% ) , Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD -0.61% ) , and Broadcom ( AVGO -0.07% ) . By comparison, OpenAI is reportedly pitching investors on annualized revenue of around $50 billion.
In other words, new cash directly affects whether those plans get paid for. And each of these chip stocks has a different amount riding on it.
Nvidia's September 2025 letter of intent covered at least 10 gigawatts of its systems, and Nvidia planned to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as each gigawatt was deployed.
The backing has since changed form. Nvidia put $30 billion into OpenAI's March round. Then in August, it agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion of obligations at an Ohio data center campus that will house Nvidia hardware under 20-year leases to OpenAI. The first guarantees aren't expected to take effect until fiscal 2029, and Nvidia's exposure drops as OpenAI pays its rent.
A well-funded OpenAI, then, lowers the odds that guarantee ever costs Nvidia anything.
Showing how much is at stake, Nvidia said every generation of its systems at that one site could mean $150 billion to $200 billion in revenue. Yet Nvidia isn't waiting on OpenAI. Its revenue climbed 106% year over year to $96.2 billion in the fiscal 2027 second quarter, which ended July 26.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $5.22T
Based on the consensus estimate for fiscal 2028 (the year through January 2028), Nvidia's price-to-earnings ratio is about 14 with shares near $217 as I write. I think that's a modest price for this much growth.
AMD's Oct. 6, 2025, deal covers 6 gigawatts of its graphics processing units (GPUs) , starting with 1 gigawatt in the second half of 2026. Chief financial officer Jean Hu put the expected payoff at "tens of billions of dollars in revenue for AMD."
"We are very happy with our strategic anchor customers in OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic. They are all in the process of ramping," CEO Lisa Su said on AMD's second-quarter earnings call in August.
Meta Platforms signed a matching 6-gigawatt deal, while Anthropic's covers up to 2 gigawatts. That leaves OpenAI with around 43% of the gigawatts across AMD's three anchor customers. And management expects data center revenue to more than double in 2027, after second-quarter sales for the segment climbed 107% year over year to $6.7 billion.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $872.95B
The stock already prices much of that in. At roughly $539 as I write, AMD's price-to-earnings ratio on 2027 consensus estimates is near 34 -- more than twice Nvidia's.
Broadcom's 10-gigawatt deal announced Oct. 13, 2025, has OpenAI designing its own artificial intelligence (AI) chips and Broadcom developing and deploying them through 2029.
Broadcom shipped Jalapeño, OpenAI's first custom accelerator, in the quarter ending Aug. 2. On the Sept. 2 earnings call, CEO Hock Tan said Jalapeño is on track for 1.3 gigawatts of deployments in 2027. And he sees OpenAI deploying over 5 gigawatts in 2028, enough to make it Broadcom's second-largest custom-chip customer.
That's when Broadcom's forecast makes its biggest dollar jump. Management expects AI chip revenue to about double to $115 billion in fiscal 2027, then double again to $230 billion in fiscal 2028.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $1.60T
But the money behind OpenAI's deployments is less settled. In June, Broadcom set up a financing vehicle with Apollo Global Management and Blackstone for OpenAI and Anthropic, and the first $35 billion goes to Anthropic's expansion. Asked about financing on the call, Tan mentioned Anthropic's path to an initial public offering .
"OpenAI, we still have less clarity, but it's different," he said.
On analysts' fiscal 2027 estimates, Broadcom's price-to-earnings ratio is around 17 with shares near $335 as of this writing.
Sure, a reported funding round isn't cash in the bank. And $30 billion is small next to OpenAI's chip plans.
Yet if the round closes, I think Broadcom gains the most, because its OpenAI financing is the least settled, and Nvidia arguably gains the least. I'd consider buying all three stocks. But with so much of AMD's plan riding on one customer at over twice Nvidia's price, I'd hold AMD as the smallest position.

items.title: Comcast Trades at 6 Times Earnings and Yields 6%. Does It Deserve to Be One of the Cheapest S&P 500 Dividend Stocks, or Is This a No-Brainer Buying Opportunity? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Comcast Trades at 6 Times Earnings and Yields 6%. Does It Deserve to Be One of the Cheapest S&P 500 Dividend Stocks, or Is This a No-Brainer Buying Opportunity?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Trading at just 6 times forward earnings and with a 6% forward dividend yield, Comcast ( CMCSA +2.10% ) stock is arguably priced for disaster. But is the super-low valuation of this telecommunications and media giant warranted, or have investors overreacted by giving the stock such a "value trap" valuation?
On one hand, there is justification for caution, given the company's ongoing broadband subscriber losses. On the other hand, with Comcast's upcoming plans to spin off the rest of its media assets, it may be on the verge of unlocking its underlying value. Or is it?
Let's take a closer look to see whether this is a prime deep-value opportunity or a name that's likely to remain a value-and-yield trap.
Broadband subscriber losses and their impact on Comcast's profitability remain key drivers of the stock's poor performance and low valuation. Comcast stopped reporting subscriber numbers this year, but as noted in a recent downgrade by KeyBanc analyst Brandon Nispel, the company is on track to lose 558,000 broadband subscribers in 2026, with another 665,000 expected to "cut the cord" with Comcast in 2027.
Nispel is not alone in his downbeat view on Comcast's dwindling subscriber base. Based on analyst estimates for 2026 and 2027 earnings, it's clear that declining subscribers, and thus declining revenue and earnings for Comcast, remain highly anticipated. Forecasts call for earnings of $3.48 and $3.59 per share in 2026 and 2027, respectively, down from $4.10 per share in 2025.
Still, it's not as if this is the sole factor at play with Comcast shares right now. After last year's spinoff of Versant Media Group ( VSNT +0.60% ) , a new entity that owns Comcast's former cable television business, Comcast plans to spin off NBCUniversal and Sky into a separate public company soon.
Analysts anticipate the market rerating these businesses separately, leading to share appreciation, even if earnings aren't set to amaze anytime soon. These bullish price targets range from $31 to $37 per share.
A major reason so many analysts still believe better times lie ahead for the stock price is recent merger activity among telecom stocks and media stocks . Following Charter Communications' purchase of Cox's cable business, there is much speculation that Comcast will merge with Charter, creating new opportunities for cost and growth synergies.

After Skydance ( SKYD +4.41% ) purchases  Warner Bros. Discovery , there's also much speculation that a larger media conglomerate could swallow up NBCUniversal after it becomes independent. However, there are no guarantees. It's unclear whether a Comcast-Charter merger would get through antitrust scrutiny.
After completing such a big transaction, I don't see Skydance rushing in to buy NBCUniversal, either. Other companies could bid for NBCUniversal, but given how peers like Walt Disney already own competing broadcast networks, finding a deep-pocketed buyer may be harder than you think.
In short, consider this catalyst highly speculative. Meanwhile, subscriber losses remain a concern, calling into question the sell side's current view that Comcast's earnings could stabilize in the coming year. Until it can fully shake off this perception, err on the side of caution and avoid the effort to bottom-fish Comcast stock .

items.title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 73 security recruits, local authorities say
items.summary: Three missiles hit a camp in government-controlled Shabwa province on Monday that was being used as a training centre, Yemen's army says.
items.content:
Image caption, Yemen's government said the missile strike killed recruits to its internal security forces (file photo)
More than 70 security personnel were killed in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa on Monday, local authorities say.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.
The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".
The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".
Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.
At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.
With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.
The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says
On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged
'We are terrified but we want to get an education', say Yemeni schoolgirls
Monday's attack in Shabwa was the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.
Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces.
A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground at the camp.
Hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and were forced to transfer the most seriously wounded people to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based, Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency.
Shabwa's media office initially reported that 53 people were killed and 200 injured in the attack.
But on Tuesday, it said in a new statement that Governor Awad bin al-Wazir had been informed by an investigative committee that the death toll was now 73, with another 14 individuals reported missing.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.
He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.
In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.
The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.
In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

items.title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
items.summary: Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue AI models.
items.content:
OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring
OpenAI has disclosed two internal coding incidents in which agents weakened the company’s misalignment monitoring safeguards.
Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months.
OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so.
An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks.
"In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech.
The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks.
OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.

items.title: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations
items.summary: U.K. inflation rose by a hotter-than-expected 3.5% in the 12 months to September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels.
items.content:
UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations
U.K. inflation jumped to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% the previous month.
Economists polled by Reuters had been forecasting an annual inflation rate of 3.4%.
Markets are pricing in two rate hikes from the Bank of England by the end of the year.
A person shields themselves from the rain while walking near the Bank of England building on the day the Monetary Policy Committee lowered interest rates, in London, Britain, Dec.18, 2025.
U.K. inflation rose by a hotter-than-expected 3.5% in the 12 months to September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels.
Economists polled by Reuters had been forecasting an annual inflation rate of 3.4%.
September's print marked a continuation of the U.K.'s upward trend for inflation, which came in at 3.1% in August and 2.9% in July. The September reading was the highest annual inflation figure in almost a year.
The U.K.'s Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that the motor fuel inflation rate had hit its highest level since August 2022, when fuel costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Britain is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks, such as the U.S.-Iran war and the subsequent struggle to move oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
U.K. motor fuel prices surged 29.8% in the year to September, ONS data showed on Wednesday.
The British pound was flat against both the euro and the U.S. dollar following the data release, and yields on U.K. government bonds were also little changed.
Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, said in a note Wednesday morning that recent growth in headline inflation had "undone the progress we saw in the spring."
"Bank of England policymakers will be looking beyond the headline figure," he said. "Services inflation, in particular, has accelerated in recent months which will create concern that we are starting to see second round inflationary effects beyond energy prices. While we face a different set of challenges compared to 2021, the prolonged conflict is weighing on the U.K. economy and making the case for a rate hike stronger."
Markets are pricing in a 98% chance that the Bank of England raises its key interest rate by 25 basis points to 4% next month, according to LSEG data, with the majority of traders also pricing in a further hike of the same size at the central bank's final meeting of the year in December.
Wednesday's expected rise in inflation also complicates the fiscal picture for the U.K. government and its finance minister.
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is set to unveil his first fiscal shakeup next week during the U.K.'s hotly anticipated Autumn Budget.
He is tasked with sticking to the previous government's so-called fiscal rules, which aim to rein in public debt while delivering on promises to soften the blow of surging consumer costs.
But separate data published Wednesday showed the U.K.'s national debt was estimated to have exceeded £3 trillion ($4 trillion) in September for the first time. The cost of servicing those debts has risen drastically over the past year, and the British economy is struggling to grow .
Healey said in a statement following Wednesday's data release that he would be "maintaining our fiscal discipline" in the budget next week, while working to "drive for growth [and give] businesses and families some breathing space."
Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said in a note Wednesday morning that rising inflation is turning the Autumn Budget into "a perilous high-wire act for the Chancellor."
He said surging prices were "increasing pressure for cost-of-living support while pushing up government borrowing costs, which is shrinking fiscal headroom and narrowing his policy options."
"With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," he said. "Policymakers will also be looking to the Chancellor to avoid adding fuel to the inflation fire by delivering a credible, fiscally disciplined Budget."

items.content:
Witkoff heads to Russia for Putin talks after Zelenskyy meeting
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff is in Russia on Wednesday for talks with President Vladimir Putin about an end to the conflict with Ukraine.
It comes after Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said late Tuesday that discussions with U.S. officials had been "constructive."
But Zelenskyy also stressed that any agreement concerning Ukraine's future would be acceptable only if Kyiv had a seat at the negotiating table.
TOPSHOT - In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin greets US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff prior to their talks in Moscow on August 6, 2025. (Photo by Gavriil Grigorov / POOL / AFP) (Photo by GAVRIIL GRIGOROV/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff is holding talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin about ending the war in Ukraine, a day after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy insisted that any negotiations over his country's future must include Kyiv.
Speaking alongside the leaders of Finland and Norway in Oslo late on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said discussions with U.S. officials had been constructive and that Washington had reaffirmed its commitment to providing Ukraine with security guarantees.
But he stressed that any agreement concerning Ukraine's future would be acceptable only if Kyiv had a seat at the negotiating table.
"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said, adding that he had discussed the reported proposal of a trilateral meeting between the U.S., China, and Russia to negotiate an end to the almost five-year conflict with U.S. representatives. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.
At the start of talks in St. Petersburg, Russia announced it would release an American man who had been "wrongfully detained," according to the State Department, on charges that he was a Ukrainian mercenary. Witkoff thanked Putin for the release of retired teacher Stephen Hubbard, according to Russian media .
(L-R) US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Finland's President Alexander Stubb, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store enter a room for a meeting on the situation in Ukraine on October 20, 2026 in Oslo. (Photo by Heiko Junge / NTB / AFP via Getty Images) / Norway OUT
On Tuesday, Zelenskyy said the Oslo meeting had included discussions on NATO's Article 5 – which says that an armed attack against one member constitutes an attack on all – and "different kinds of security guarantees," which Witkoff will share with the Russians. "We will hear his feedback in one day," Zelenskyy said Tuesday.
The developments come amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine as President Donald Trump and Zelenskyy have traded public criticism. Trump has accused the Ukrainian president of not wanting peace, while Zelenskyy has argued that Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia, including a deal on diesel , risks prolonging the conflict.
Overnight, Russia struck energy and civilian targets across Ukraine, resulting in at least one casualty, according to local media reports. It follows Trump's Oct. 11 claim that he had brokered an "energy ceasefire," whereby the countries would refrain from striking each other's energy infrastructure amid high diesel prices.
Ukraine paused such attacks for three days before resuming them, citing continuing Russian attacks.
On Tuesday, Zelenskyy confirmed that U.S. intelligence had resumed sharing early warnings of Russian attacks, while discussions continued over SpaceX's Starlink connectivity and Patriot air defense systems.
